questions.prompt: Where does a good workload model mostly get its numbers?
options: Production analytics and logs for peak periods, plus business forecasts
questions.explanation: Real usage data, especially at peak, is the best source; forecasts adjust it for growth or events.

questions.prompt: Think time represents the pause a real user takes between actions, such as reading a page.
questions.explanation: Think time keeps the request rate per user realistic. Without it, each virtual user behaves like a script hammering the server.

questions.prompt: Peak hour: 54,000 product views, 9,000 add-to-cart, 1,800 checkouts. What share of the mix is checkout?
questions.explanation: Total = 64,800. 1,800 / 64,800 ≈ 0.0278, about 2.8%. Mix percentages must come from the same period.

Which details belong in a workload model? Select all that apply.
options: Transaction mix and rates at peak
Data variety (e.g. number of distinct products and users)
questions.explanation: Mix, rates, pacing and data distribution all affect load; people's names do not.

questions.prompt: Production analytics show 80% of traffic arrives in a 15-minute burst after a daily email. The test uses the daily average rate. What is the problem?
options: The test underestimates peak load by a large factor; model the burst rate (and ramp) instead of the daily average
The test should use 24 hours of think time
questions.explanation: Systems fail at peaks. A daily average flattens the burst that actually stresses the system.

questions.prompt: A public API's clients send requests independently of how fast the API responds. Which load model should the test use, and why?
options: An open model (fixed arrival rate), because real arrivals do not slow down when the system slows, so queues build up as they would in production
A closed model with few users, because it is simpler
Any model; results are the same
questions.explanation: Closed models self-throttle when responses slow, hiding overload. Open models match independent arrivals and reveal it.
